faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other such that, from our viewpoint on Earth, one star periodically passes in front of the other. When this happens, the combined brightness dips. By measuring these dips in a light curve - a record of brightness over time - we can learn about the stars' sizes, orbital period, and brightness ratio.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?

faqs.answer: A 'candidate' is a star whose light curve shows statistical signatures of an eclipsing binary but has not yet been checked for contamination. A 'confirmed' candidate has passed an automated pixel-level check that verifies the brightness changes originate from the target star itself and are not caused by nearby background stars or instrumental artifacts. Confirmation here means it passed this technical check - not that it has been scientifically characterized or verified by independent means.
faqs.question: What do you mean by 'candidate' versus 'confirmed'?

faqs.answer: The ML score is a second opinion on candidate quality, generated by a machine-learning model trained on nearly 3,000 labeled examples. It outperforms the baseline statistical approach used by the pipeline. The score is informational and reflects how well the candidate matches patterns in the training set - it is not used to decide which candidates get the pixel-level check, and it does not gate or filter the results shown on this site.
faqs.question: What is the machine-learning score I see listed?

faqs.answer: The pixel-level check is a fully automated process that examines whether the measured brightness change comes from the target star or from contaminating sources such as nearby stars or instrumental issues. It does not involve manual or visual inspection. Candidates that pass this check are listed as confirmed on this site.
faqs.question: How does the pixel-level check work?

faqs.answer: The period-alias check compares the depths of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If these depths differ significantly, it may indicate that the measured orbital period is an alias - a harmonic or fractional multiple of the true period. When this check raises a flag, a caveat is noted on the candidate's individual page.
faqs.question: What is the period-alias check?

faqs.answer: Yes. TESS light-curve data are publicly available, and the orbital periods and eclipse depths reported here can be checked against the raw data. You can also visually inspect the light curve on each candidate's page to form your own assessment.
faqs.question: Can I verify a candidate's result myself?

faqs.answer: Being listed here represents the end of what this automated pipeline does. The pipeline measures orbital period and relative eclipse depths from the light curve. It does not perform spectroscopy, radial-velocity measurement, or any other follow-up characterization. Candidates may be pursued by other researchers, but any such activity lies outside this project.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed on this site?

faqs.answer: Each candidate passes multiple automated quality gates: statistical vetting of the light curve, a cross-check against six major catalogs to confirm it is not already known, and a pixel-level check to rule out contamination. The machine-learning model provides an additional layer of confidence by outperforming the baseline approach. That said, some candidates may carry caveats noted on their individual pages - the pipeline identifies strong signals, but follow-up work can refine or revise any particular result.
faqs.question: Why should I trust these results?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from the TESS satellite. Eclipsing binaries are pairs of stars that orbit each other and periodically pass in front of each other as seen from Earth, causing dips in brightness we can measure in light curves. The pipeline starts with over 20,000 target stars, applies statistical quality checks, cross-references six major variable-star catalogs to flag novel objects, and runs an automated pixel-level check to confirm that brightness changes come from the target star itself rather than nearby background sources. Of these, 284 candidates have passed the pixel-level check. A machine-learning model trained on nearly 3,000 labeled examples provides a second opinion on candidate quality, outperforming the baseline statistical approach. Each confirmed candidate is listed here with its measured orbital period and eclipse depths, along with any caveats noted during vetting. This systematic approach yields a high-confidence sample suitable for follow-up characterization.
